entries.0ea3e8590cb23cd21d6f91a4004ae0b4013d58a4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.4.24" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Rom.4.24" sID="gen113709" type="section"/> <div sID="gen113710" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24.</hi> <hi type="italic">Who believe on him</hi>, <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> I have already reminded you of the design of those periphrastic expressions: Paul introduced them, that he might, according to what the passages may require, describe in various ways the real character of faith — of which the resurrection of Christ is not the smallest part; for it is the ground of our hope as to eternal life. Had he said only, that we believe in God, it could not have been so readily learnt how this could serve to obtain righteousness; but when Christ comes forth and presents to us in his own resurrection a sure pledge of life, it then appears evident from what fountain the imputation of righteousness flows.<div eID="gen113710" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.4.24" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen113709" osisID="Rom.4.24" type="section"/>

25. Who was delivered for our offences,
It is διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα ἡμων, “for our offenses,” and διὰ τὴν δικαίωσιν ἡμων, “for our justification.” The preposition διὰ, has here clearly two meanings: the first signifies the reason why, and the second, the end for which. How is this to be known? By the character of the sentence, and by what is taught elsewhere. For, to which Johnson attaches forty meanings, is commonly understood here as having a different sense, and this is sufficiently indicated by what is connected with it. But in case a doubt arises, we have only to consult other passages in which the subject is handled.
Take the first instance — “for our offenses.” There are those who say that διὰ here means because of, or, on account of; and this, in order to evade the idea of a propitiation. The preposition, no doubt, has this sense; but is this its sense here? If the sentence itself be deemed insufficient to determine the question, (though to a plain reader it is,) let us see what is said elsewhere of Christ’s death in connection with our sins or offenses. He himself said, that he came “to give his life a ransom (λύτρον — a redeeming price) for many,” Matthew 20:28. It is said, that he “gave himself a ransom (ἀντίλυτρον — a redeeming price for another) for all,” 1 Timothy 2:6. It is expressly declared, that “Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many,” Hebrews 9:28. And more to the purpose still, if possible, is the testimony of John, when he says that Christ “is the propitiation (ἱλασμός — expiation) for our sins,” 1 John 2:2. Now, can it be that we can give any other meaning to the text, than that God delivered his Son as a sacrifice for our offenses? This is the doctrine of Scripture throughout. — Ed.
etc. He expands and illustrates more at large the doctrine to which I have just referred. It indeed greatly concerns us, not only to have our minds directed to Christ, but also to have it distinctly made known how he attained salvation for us. And though Scripture, when it treats of our salvation, dwells especially on the death of Christ, yet the Apostle now proceeds farther: for as his purpose was more explicitly to set forth the cause of our salvation, he mentions its two parts; and says, first, that our sins were expiated by the death of Christ, — and secondly, that by his resurrection was obtained our righteousness. But the meaning is, that when we possess the benefit of Christ’s death and resurrection, there is nothing wanting to the completion of perfect righteousness. By separating his death from his resurrection, he no doubt accommodates what he says to our ignorance; for it is also true that righteousness has been obtained for us by that obedience of Christ, which he exhibited in his death, as the Apostle himself teaches us in the following chapter. But as Christ, by rising from the dead, made known how much he had effected by his death, this distinction is calculated to teach us that our salvation was begun by the sacrifice, by which our sins were expiated, and was at length completed by his resurrection: for the beginning of righteousness is to be reconciled to God, and its completion is to attain life by having death abolished. Paul then means, that satisfaction for our sins was given on the cross: for it was necessary, in order that Christ might restore us to the Father’s favor, that our sins should be abolished by him; which could not have been done had he not on their account suffered the punishment, which we were not equal to endure. Hence Isaiah says, that the chastisement of our peace was upon him. (Isaiah 53:5.) But he says that he was delivered, and not, that he died; for expiation depended on the eternal goodwill of God, who purposed to be in this way pacified.
And was raised again for our justification. As it would not have been enough for Christ to undergo the wrath and judgment of God, and to endure the curse due to our sins, without his coming forth a conqueror, and without being received into celestial glory, that by his intercession he might reconcile God to us, the efficacy of justification is ascribed to his resurrection, by which death was overcome; not that the sacrifice of the cross, by which we are reconciled to God, contributes nothing towards our justification, but that the completeness of his favor appears more clear by his coming to life again.
Christ is said here to have been raised from the dead by God, as well as delivered into death. “However much of the import of this,” says Chalmers, “may have escaped the notice of an ordinary reader, it is pregnant with meaning of the weightiest importance. You know that when the prison door is opened to a criminal, and that by the very authority which lodged him there, it envinces that the debt of his transgression has been rendered, and that he stands aquitted of all it’s penalties. It was not for his own, but for our offenses that Jesus was delivered unto the death, and that his body was consigned to the imprisonment of the grave. And when an angel descended from heaven, and rolled back the great stone from the door of the sepulchre, this speaks to us, that the justice of God is satisfied, that the ransom of our iniquity has been paid, that Christ has rendered a full discharge of all the debt for which he undertook as the great surety between God and the sinners who believe in him.” — Ed.
But I cannot assent to those who refer this second clause to newness of life; for of that the Apostle has not begun to speak; and further, it is certain that both clauses refer to the same thing. For if justification means renovation, then that he died for our sins must be taken in the same sense, as signifying that he acquired for us grace to mortify the flesh; which no one admits. Then, as he is said to have died for our sins, because he delivered us from the evil of death by suffering death as a punishment for our sins; so he is now said to have been raised for our justification, because he fully restored life to us by his resurrection: for he was first smitten by the hand of God, that in the person of the sinner he might sustain the misery of sin; and then he was raised to life, that he might freely grant to his people righteousness and life.
“Either therefore as the evidence of the acceptance of his suffering as our substitute, or as a necessary step toward securing the application of their merit to our benefit, the resurrection of Christ was essential to our justification.” — Professor Hodge
He therefore still speaks of imputative justification; and this will be confirmed by what immediately follows in the next chapter.
CHAPTER 5
Romans 5:1-2

1. Iustificatus ergo ex fide, pacem habemus apud Deum per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum;

2. Per quem accessum habiumus fide in gratiam istam in qua stetimus, et gloriamur super spe gloriæ Dei.

And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 17.10.</ns0:note> he receiv'd the sign <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or <ns0:hi>Circumcision</ns0:hi> which is a <ns0:hi>Sign.</ns0:hi> Two Things are here Affirm'd of <ns0:hi>circumcision:</ns0:hi> 1. That it was a <ns0:hi>Seal</ns0:hi>; Of what? <ns0:hi>Of the Righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness of Faith:</ns0:hi> Of the meaning of which, see the Notes on <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.17. Rom.</ns0:hi> 10.6. and the Notes there. <ns0:hi>Circumcision</ns0:hi> is called a <ns0:hi>Seal,</ns0:hi> because it was a Confirmation of the <ns0:hi>Cove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nant of Grace,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Righteousness</ns0:hi> therein promis'd. The common Use of a Seal amongst Men is to Confirm and Ratify a Matter, and make it more Firm and Sure: It is joyn'd often with an Earnest, which is for the same end and purpose. The <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> Conversion is said to be the <ns0:hi>Seal</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi>'s Apostleship, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> It was a Confirmation of i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> and made it more Evident that he was <ns0:hi>Sent of God.</ns0:hi> What the Apostle sayes of an <ns0:hi>Oath,</ns0:hi> that we may say of a <ns0:hi>Seal</ns0:hi>; It is for Confirmation, and for putting things out of Controversy. When God made a <ns0:hi>Promise</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> He Confirm'd it with an <ns0:hi>Oath</ns0:hi>; and when He made a <ns0:hi>Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venant</ns0:hi> with him, and with his Seed, He Confirm'd it by a <ns0:hi>Seal,</ns0:hi> and that was <ns0:hi>Circumcision</ns0:hi>; which he calls in <ns0:hi>Genesis</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Covenant of God,</ns0:hi> and here the <ns0:hi>Seal</ns0:hi> thereof. And what is said of <ns0:hi>circumcision,</ns0:hi> is not spoken of it barely as <ns0:hi>circumcision,</ns0:hi> but as a <ns0:hi>Sacrament</ns0:hi>; and it shews the Nature and Use of all <ns0:hi>Sacraments,</ns0:hi> both of the <ns0:hi>Old-Testament</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>New</ns0:hi>; that they are <ns0:hi>Seals</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>New Covenant.</ns0:hi> That which the Apostle mentions here of <ns0:hi>circumcision,</ns0:hi> hath nothing Proper and Pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />culiar in it to <ns0:hi>circumcision</ns0:hi> as such; but it may, with equal Reason, be apply'd to any other <ns0:hi>Sacrament;</ns0:hi> It belongs as well to the <ns0:hi>Passover,</ns0:hi> yea to <ns0:hi>Baptism,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Lords Supper, e. g.</ns0:hi> The Apostle first calls <ns0:hi>Circumcision</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Sign,</ns0:hi> so was the <ns0:hi>Passover,</ns0:hi> so is <ns0:hi>Baptism,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Lords Supper.</ns0:hi> Again, he calls it <ns0:hi>A Seal of the Righteousness of Faith,</ns0:hi> or of the <ns0:hi>New-Covenant,</ns0:hi> as before. And so is each of the other <ns0:hi>Sacra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments</ns0:hi>; take for instance the <ns0:hi>Lords-Supper:</ns0:hi> Our Saviour calls the Cup therein the <ns0:hi>New-Testament</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Covenant,</ns0:hi> that is, It is a <ns0:hi>Seal</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Confirmation</ns0:hi> thereof. And what is here Affirm'd of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> may be Affirm'd as well of the <ns0:hi>Eu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nuch,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Iayhor,</ns0:hi> or any <ns0:hi>Baptiz'd Person</ns0:hi>; he receiv'd the <ns0:hi>Sign of Baptism, a Seal of the Righteousness of Faith,</ns0:hi> and of <ns0:hi>Remission of Sins,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> of circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith, which <ns0:hi>he had yet</ns0:hi> being uncircumcised: that he might be the father <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> That he might be Known or Declared to be the <ns0:hi>Father</ns0:hi> of such; see the like Phrase <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 5.45. Though many of the Fathers did Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve before <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> yet none of them are said to be the <ns0:hi>Fathers of the Faithful,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> was, because God made to none of them the like Promise, concerning their Poste<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity, as he did to <ns0:hi>Abraham.</ns0:hi> See the next Verse.</ns0:note> of all them that believe, though they be not circumcised; that righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness might be imputed to them also.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12. And the father of circumcision to them who are not of the circumcision onely, but who also walk in the steps of that faith of our father Abraham <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">The former Verse tells you he was the <ns0:hi>Father</ns0:hi> of the Believing <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> for the <ns0:hi>Covenant</ns0:hi> was made with him, for all his <ns0:hi>Believing Seed,</ns0:hi> when he was <ns0:hi>Vncircumcised,</ns0:hi> which shews, That <ns0:hi>Righteousness</ns0:hi> is, and may be <ns0:hi>imputed to them also,</ns0:hi> without any outward <ns0:hi>Circumcision</ns0:hi>; and then he is the <ns0:hi>Father</ns0:hi> of the Believing <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi>; especially of as many of them, as unto <ns0:hi>circumcision,</ns0:hi> do add the Imitation of his <ns0:hi>Faith.</ns0:hi> Who (besides <ns0:hi>circumcision</ns0:hi> which they deriv'd from him) do also Transcribe his divine Copy, and follow his Example of Faith and Obedience: That leave their Sins, as he did his Country; that Believe all God's Promises, and adhere to him against all Temptations to the contrary.</ns0:note>, which <ns0:hi>he had</ns0:hi> being <ns0:hi>yet</ns0:hi> uncircum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cised.</ns0:p>

                     <ns0:hi>A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />braham should be the Father of all that Believe,</ns0:hi> whither of the <ns0:hi>circumcision</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>uncircumcision.</ns0:hi> Others by the <ns0:hi>World,</ns0:hi> do un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstand the <ns0:hi>Land of Canaan</ns0:hi>; under which also, Heaven was typically Promised and Comprehended, <ns0:hi>vid.                      <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> It was not made to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> because he had merited it by keeping the <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi>; but because he had believed God, and obtain'd the <ns0:hi>Righteousness of Faith.</ns0:hi> In the whole Verse is couch'd an Argument for <ns0:hi>Iustification by Faith without Works,</ns0:hi> which is the Apostles drift; and it may be thus form'd, If the Promise of Inheritance to <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> and his <ns0:hi>Seed,</ns0:hi> was to be accomplisht not by Legal Obedience, but by the <ns0:hi>Righteousness of Faith</ns0:hi>; then it follows, That <ns0:hi>We are Iustified by Faith, and not by Works</ns0:hi>; but the Promise of In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />heritance to <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> and his Seed, was to be Accomplish't, not by the Law, but by the <ns0:hi>Righteousness of Faith.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> If they which seek the <ns0:hi>Inhe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritance of the Law,</ns0:hi> can by the <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> obtain it, then there is no use of <ns0:hi>Faith:</ns0:hi> To what end should we <ns0:hi>by Faith</ns0:hi> go out of our selves to <ns0:hi>seek Righteousness and Salvation in Christ,</ns0:hi> if we could obtain it by the Legal Obedience.                      <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Promise it self, which was made to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> and his Seed; that also is ineffec<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tual, and brought to nought; no Man shall be Saved by it.                      <ns0:hi>i. e.                      <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Wrath of God:</ns0:hi> And this it doth not of its self, but occasionally in Respect of our Disobedience. This is a Confirmation of what was said in the foregoing Verse: That the Inheritance is not by the <ns0:hi>Law,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Works thereof</ns0:hi>; he proves it from the Effect and <ns0:hi>Work</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Law,</ns0:hi> such as it hath in all Men since the <ns0:hi>Fall</ns0:hi>; it <ns0:hi>worketh Wrath,</ns0:hi> it is so far from entituling Men to the Promis'd Blessing that it exposeth Men to the Curse and Wrath of God, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.10.</ns0:note>: For where no law is, <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> no transgression <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> And that it <ns0:hi>worketh Wrath</ns0:hi> is Evident, because it discovers and occasions <ns0:hi>Trangressions,</ns0:hi> betwixt which, and God's Wrath, there is an inseparable Connecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on. This Assertion is simply True, of things indifferent, as were all Ceremonial Observations before the <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired them; for then before the <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> it was no Sin to Omit them: But of things which are Evil in their own nature, it must be understood Respectively, and after a sort. That is, there was no such great <ns0:hi>Transgression</ns0:hi> before the <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> was given, as afterwards. As also, Because by the <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> comes the clear Knowledge of Man's Duty, and so the Servant that knows his Masters Will, and doth it not, is worthy of the more Stripes.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  </ns0:note> all the seed, <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>'s Seed is of two Sorts. One Sort is of the <ns0:hi>Law,</ns0:hi> to wit, the <ns0:hi>Iews.</ns0:hi> Another Sort is, of such as walk in the Steps of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Faith,</ns0:hi> whither <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Gentiles.</ns0:hi> To all these the <ns0:hi>Promise must be sure</ns0:hi>; which cannot be, if the <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> be made the Condition or Means of the In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />heritance.</ns0:note> not to that only which is of the law, but to that also which is of the faith of Abraham, <ns0:note place="margin">

                  </ns0:note> before him whom he believed <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In the Sight of Esteem of God. He was not the <ns0:hi>Father of many Nations</ns0:hi> by Carnal Generation in the sight of Men, but by Spiritual Cognation in the Sight of God. Or as it may be read, <ns0:hi>Like unto God,</ns0:hi> after his Example; and then the meaning is, That God so Honoured <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Faith,</ns0:hi> that He made him a <ns0:hi>Father,</ns0:hi> in some respects like Himself: As God is an Universal <ns0:hi>Father,</ns0:hi> not of One, but of all Nations, so was <ns0:hi>Abraham.</ns0:hi> Again, As God is their <ns0:hi>Spiritual Father,</ns0:hi> not by Carnal Generation, so was <ns0:hi>Abra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ham</ns0:hi> also.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> God who quickneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were:<ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e. Abraham believed</ns0:hi> in Him as Omnipotent. His Omnipotency is described by two great Effects of it. The One in making that to have a Being again, which had ceas'd to be, as in the <ns0:hi>Resurrection.</ns0:hi> The other, in cau<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing that to be, which never was; or to make all Things of Nothing, as in the <ns0:hi>Creation:</ns0:hi> He Expresseth this by cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling Things, to intimate the great Facility of this <ns0:hi>Work</ns0:hi> to God. <ns0:hi>He only spoke, and it was done; He commanded, and all was created.</ns0:hi> And as <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> thus generally <ns0:hi>be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieved</ns0:hi> the Power of God, so 'tis likely he made a particu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lar Application of it, to his own State at present; as he <ns0:hi>believed</ns0:hi> that God could raise the Dead<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> so that He could Raise him Seed out of his own dead Body, and <ns0:hi>Sarah</ns0:hi>'s dead Womb.                <ns0:p n="19">19. And being not weak in Faith, <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">

                     </ns0:gap> 11. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 11,</ns0:note> he con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sidered <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">He regarded not the Impotency of <ns0:hi>his own Body,</ns0:hi> which was, as it were <ns0:hi>dead,</ns0:hi> because of his Age, in respect of any desires or powers of Generation. <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> several years after Marryed <ns0:hi>Keturah,</ns0:hi> by whom he had divers Children, How then doth the Apostle say his <ns0:hi>body</ns0:hi> was <ns0:hi>now dead,</ns0:hi> or unable for Generation? Some say that the deadness of <ns0:hi>Abrahams body</ns0:hi> was only in his own Opinion. <ns0:hi>Augustine</ns0:hi> hath two Answers. 1. That <ns0:hi>his body</ns0:hi> was not <ns0:hi>dead</ns0:hi> simply, but in respect of <ns0:hi>Sarah,</ns0:hi> he might be able to beget Children<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of a younger Woman. 2. His body was revived, and he receiv'd a new Generative Faculty of God. Another question may be mov'd, and that is, how the Apostle could say that <ns0:hi>Abraham considered not his own body,</ns0:hi> being <ns0:hi>dead?</ns0:hi> seeing we read, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 17.17. that <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> upon the promise of a Son, fell upon his face and laughed, and said in his heart, Shall a Child be born unto him that is <ns0:hi>an Hundred years Old?</ns0:hi> &c. Some answer that <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> at first doubted, but afterwards he recollected himself, and got over that unbelief, his <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> overcame all diffi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />culties: others say, that he doubted not at all of the truth of Gods Promise, but was uncertain only how it should be understood, whither properly or figuratively, <ns0:hi>vid. Gen.</ns0:hi> 17.19. Others say, that these words of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> are not words of doubting, but enquiring; they proceed from a desire to be farther instructed, how that thing should be. It was a Question like that of the Virgin <ns0:hi>Mary's. How shall these things be?</ns0:hi> Augustine <ns0:hi>sayes, That</ns0:hi> Abrahams <ns0:hi>laugh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter was not like</ns0:hi> Sarahs. Hers proceeded from Distrust, His from Joy and Admiration.</ns0:note> not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sarahs womb.</ns0:p>

Rom. 14.23. <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> James 1.6. <ns0:hi>'tis rendred Wa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vering.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> staggered not at the promise of God <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 15.5. & 17.16.</ns0:note>, through unbelief: but was strong in faith, giving glory to God:<ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">As all do that rely upon the Power and <ns0:hi>Promise of God,</ns0:hi> setting to their Seals that He is True.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21. And being fully perswaded, that what he had promised, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psa. 115.3<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> he was able also to per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />form <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">He lookt upon God as one that was perfectly able to do what ever <ns0:hi>he had promised,</ns0:hi> and as one that was most faithful and sure never to fail in the performance; collecting nothing else from the difficulty and impro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bability of the matter, but that it was the fitter for an Almighty Power to effect.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22. And therefore it was imputed to him for Righteousness <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>vid. v.</ns0:hi> 3. By reason of <ns0:hi>his Faith</ns0:hi> he was as suffici<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ently disposed and qualified for the obtaining of the pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mise, as if he had had all the <ns0:hi>Righteousness</ns0:hi> required by the Law.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23. Now it <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1. Cor. 10.6<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 11.</ns0:note> was not written for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24. But for us also, to whom it shall be im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />puted, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead.<ns0:note place="bottom">Here it may be enquired. If <ns0:hi>Abraham's Faith</ns0:hi> did justi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fie him, <ns0:hi>and it was imputed to him for Righteousness,</ns0:hi> what doth this concern us? The Apostle Answers it was recorded of him for our sakes. <ns0:hi>vid.</ns0:hi> Chap. 15.4. And to us there shall be the like imputation, if we believe in God, <ns0:hi>that raised up Iesus our Lord from the dead.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">This is a greater Act of <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> than <ns0:hi>Abraham's</ns0:hi> was. And the nature of justifying <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> lies rather in aff<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ance, or in putting trust in God through our <ns0:hi>Lord Iesus Christ,</ns0:hi> then in assent or in giving credit to the Truth of his promise. <ns0:hi>Q.</ns0:hi> Why doth the Apostle sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gle out this Act of raising Christ from the dead to describe the Father by? <ns0:hi>A.</ns0:hi> To maintain the proportion betwixt the <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> of his Seed; that as his respected the Power of God, in raising (as it were) the dead, so in like sort should ours. So some. But the A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postle speaks, as if there were some special reason and ground for confidence in God for justification in this Act of raising Christ from the dead; and indeed nothing is more fit to establish our Faith in perswasion of our justification than this; for when God raised up our <ns0:hi>Lord Iesus Christ,</ns0:hi> having loosed the pains of death, he gave full assurance, that his Justice is fully satisfied for our sins. Had not <ns0:hi>Christ Iesus</ns0:hi> our surety paid the utmost farthing that was due for our sins, he had still continued in prison, and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the power of death. Hence 'tis that the Apostle <ns0:hi>Pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter</ns0:hi> tells us, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.3. <ns0:hi>That God hath begotten us to a lively hope of the Heavenly Inheritance by the Resurrection of Christ from the dead</ns0:hi>; there being no more effectual means to perswade us of the pardon of sin, of reconcilia<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion with God, and of acceptance to eternal Life, then that Jesus Christ our surety and sponsor is risen from the dead.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>

                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> for the expiating of them. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 53.10.</ns0:note>, and was raised again for our justification <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Not that his death had no hand in <ns0:hi>our justification. vid. Rom.</ns0:hi> 3.24. but because our <ns0:hi>justification</ns0:hi> which was begun in his Death, was perfected in his Resurection. Christ did meritoriously work <ns0:hi>our justification</ns0:hi> and salvation by his Death and Passion, but the efficacy and perfection there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />of with respect to us, dependeth on his Resurrection. By his Death he paid our debt, in his Resurrection he received our acquittance, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 53.8. when he was discharged, we in him, & together with him received our discharge from the guilt and punishment of all our sins.
